en.body:
## A Bold Swing at Satire

**Alejandro G. Iñárritu** has never shied away from grand artistic statements, and his latest offering, **Digger**, is no exception. The film, starring **Tom Cruise** as the titular character, attempts a biting satire aimed at the right-wing ruling class and the absurdities of our current socio-political climate. Set against a backdrop where even comedy is deemed "legal" only after considerable political upheaval, **Digger** questions how future generations might process the troubles of our times through art, especially when billionaires hold the purse strings. While the film raises these compelling questions, reviews suggest it doesn't always provide satisfying answers, instead prompting post-viewing conversations.

Despite its thematic ambitions, **Digger** is described as "stale but never boring." The stylistic choices, including a desaturated color palette and a score that shifts between whimsical and orchestral, have been called "off-putting but never boring." The narrative reportedly involves a precarious situation with an iceberg, leading to drastic measures like using AI to ban contentious words and even contemplating a nuclear option. The fallout culminates in **Digger**'s impassioned speech to the European parliament, a moment that, while potentially predictable, is far from dull.

## Fan and Critic Reactions

The film's reception has been a mixed bag, with some praising **Iñárritu**'s technique and **Tom Cruise**'s performance, while others find it to be an "embarrassing miss." The New Yorker notes **Cruise**'s portrayal as both "scream-inducing and gas-inducing," highlighting the interplay of camera and scenery. Conversely, some online discussions liken **Digger** to its protagonist, calling it "arrogant and pompous" and believing it to be "smarter than its audience." The specifics of the film's plot have been kept under wraps, with **Iñárritu** reportedly requesting critics not to reveal certain aspects, a move that has only added to the intrigue and speculation surrounding the movie.

## What's Next

While specific release details for **Digger** beyond its festival debut are still emerging, audiences eager for **Alejandro G. Iñárritu**'s latest directorial effort and **Tom Cruise**'s venture into dark satire will want to stay tuned for wider theatrical or streaming announcements. The film's divisive nature suggests it's poised to be a major talking point in the cinematic world.

content_raw: Many were optimistic that the first Trump Presidential term would be, at the very least, a blessing for satire. Two years into his second term and a former member of his cabinet was the one to declare comedy “legal” again, and the most lightweight of comedians were forced off the air in attempts by the networks to ally themselves with his administration further. This is the cultural context that kept circling around my mind while watching Digger , a movie that raises questions about whether the troubles of our times will be processed by future generations through art, and what that can possibly look like, considering the billionaires holding the purse strings. Unfortunately, it doesn’t satisfyingly explore these ideas so much as raise them so the audience can have a more invigorating post-viewing conversation; David Ellison may not be in control of Warner Bros. just yet, but even he would shrug off this satire aimed at the right-wing ruling class if he were in charge when the project arrived at his desk. The specifics of how the movie approaches these ideas is being treated as a spoiler, which director Alejandro G. Iñárritu has explicitly asked critics not to reveal in all invitations sent to the press—maybe the first case of a director willing an F Cinemascore upon himself. Personally speaking, I found this unrevealed aspect of the movie far less interesting than the face-value shenanigans teased in the trailer, its bolder s various projections that rely on the whims of wind and ocean currents, and his administration instead opts to use an AI to ban contentious words ranging from “ice” to “Al Gore” on social media. It was either that or drop a nuke on the iceberg. The beat-by-beat fallout, which builds up to Digger’s impassioned speech to the booing members of the European parliament about how his company supplies their “freedom” (itself an unintentional echo of the far better Foghorn Leghorn courtroom monologue in last month’s Coyote vs. Acme ), may be predictable for anybody with an interest in more realist post-apocalyptic dramas such as Threads , but it’s never boring. Cruise and Ahmed both locate the right tone for the director’s brand of over-the-top dark comedy, finding just the ideal amount of silliness in the seriousness, working best when bouncing off each other. The same can’t be said of the rest of the supporting ensemble, especially a well-cast but badly-utilized Goodman, who has been cursed with a character written as if all his uses of curse words were the jokes in and of themselves. The movie threatens to become a tiresome edgelord shock fest each time he reminds someone he has “cancer of the asshole.”  For reasons I can’t get into, Digger insulates itself from the criticism of being unsatisfyingly broad satire, to the extent this is even called out within the text.
